name: TDengine
workload: IoTDB-benchmark (Tsinghua THULAB harness, forked by the TickTock author) wind-farm IoT workload, mixed 9:1 write:read, 300 clients x 300 devices x 10 sensors (TimescaleDB 10 clients x 10 devices x 100 sensors), each database in a Docker container pinned to 2 vCPU and 4 GB.
claimed_speedup: Write throughput (datapoint/s): TDengine 629,904 vs InfluxDB 74,534 (about 8.5x, derived from page data) and vs TimescaleDB 112,494 (about 5.6x, derived from page data). Read throughput table (Precise_point / Time_range / Agg_range / Group_by / Latest_point): TDengine 59 / 3035 / 60 / 805 / 140 vs InfluxDB 17 / 829 / 17 / 17 / 17 vs TimescaleDB 1 / 63 / 1 / 16 / 1. Memory: TDengine used the smallest RSS, about 500 MB, vs about 1 GB for InfluxDB and nearly the full 4 GB for TimescaleDB.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt Docker images, no compilation: tdengine/tdengine:2.0.22.0, influxdb:2.0, timescale/timescaledb:latest-pg12 (reported as 2.6.0-pg12); docker run --cpuset-cpus 0-1 -m 4g; TimescaleDB max_connections raised.
hardware: Ideapad gaming laptop: AMD Ryzen 5 5600H (6 cores / 12 threads), 20 GB DDR4-3200, 1 TB 5400 RPM HDD, Ubuntu 20.04.3; benchmark client on the same machine.
stars_or_usage: 25.2k stars; README cites over 730k running instances
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 copyleft (network-use clause) for the open-source tree. Time-series specific data model (super tables and sub-tables per device) and TDengine SQL rather than a general SQL engine. README says Linux is the primary platform, with limited Windows support in the open-source tree.
caveats: The only numeric TDengine-vs-InfluxDB/TimescaleDB comparison I could open is a third-party wiki written by the author of a rival time-series database (TickTock), who wins the same chart, not TDengine's own report. The wiki text gives only TickTock and IoTDB write numbers and the TDengine 500 MB memory figure; the TDengine/InfluxDB/TimescaleDB numbers quoted here were read from the wiki's result images (througput_w.jpg and througput_tbl.jpg in the ylin30/ticktock-wiki repo), and the read-throughput table header is cropped so its unit is not visible. Old TDengine 2.0.22.0 (2.x line, long before the current 3.x) and InfluxDB 2.0 were tested on a laptop with a 5400 RPM HDD in 2-vCPU containers; TimescaleDB used a different workload shape (10 clients, 100-sensor batches) that the wiki itself calls unfair to the others; TDengine ran 1M loops versus 100K for InfluxDB and TimescaleDB; the harness is a modified fork of IoTDB-benchmark (connection pools added), which I did not open. TDengine's own TSBS reports on tdengine.com (search-result snippet only, page blocked here, not opened) claim ingestion 1.5x to 6.7x faster than TimescaleDB and 3.0x to 10.6x faster than InfluxDB; an arXiv paper 'Benchmarking Specialized Databases for High-frequency Data' (snippet only, not opened) reports TDengine at 1.63M rows/s vs TimescaleDB 343K rows/s. The category is a best fit: TDengine is a time-series database, not a message queue. Tier B is generous (independent but not peer reviewed, harness not inspected); a verifier may prefer C.

name: Zvec
baseline: Milvus 2.5.11 (sq8) and Milvus 2.2.12 (HNSW), plus Zilliz Cloud (managed Milvus) 8cu-perf v2025.6, via VectorDBBench
workload: VectorDBBench Cohere 10M (10 million 768-dimensional vectors, HNSW m=50, ef-search 118, int8 quantization with refiner) and Cohere 1M (HNSW m=15, ef-search 180, int8), QPS at concurrency 12-20 on a 16 vCPU / 64 GiB instance.
claimed_speedup: Cohere 10M QPS: Zvec 8,475 vs Milvus-16c64g-sq8-2.5.11 437.2 (about 19x, derived from page data), vs Milvus-16c64g-hnsw-v2.2.12 178.7 (about 47x, derived from page data), vs ZillizCloud-8cu-perf-v2025.6 3,957 (about 2.1x, derived from page data). Cohere 1M QPS: Zvec 16,490 vs Milvus-16c64g-sq8-2.5.11 3,465 (about 4.8x, derived), vs Milvus-16c64g-hnsw-v2.2.12 1,259 (about 13x, derived), vs ZillizCloud-8cu-perf-v2025.6 9,704 (about 1.7x, derived). Load duration Cohere 10M: Zvec 3,894 s vs ZillizCloud 5,682 s, Milvus hnsw 5,714 s, Milvus sq8 8,564 s.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt PyPI wheel (pip install zvec==v0.1.1), no compiler flags stated; run as 'vectordbbench zvec ... --quantize-type int8 --m 50 --ef-search 118 --is-using-refiner' (10M) and '--m 15 --ef-search 180' (1M).
hardware: Alibaba Cloud ECS g9i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 64 GiB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04; CPU model not named.
stars_or_usage: 16.1k stars; used inside Alibaba Group, built on Proxima
tradeoffs: In-process embedded library: no server, but writes are single-process exclusive (multiple processes may read the same collection). Benchmarked configuration trades recall for speed with int8 quantization plus a refiner. SDKs for Python, Node.js, Go, Rust and Dart.
caveats: First-party numbers. The docs site zvec.org and the chart host were blocked, so the figures were read from the chart images embedded in the SVGs of the zvec-ai/zvec-web docs repo (qps-10M.svg, recall-10M.svg, load-duration-10M.svg, qps-1M.svg, recall-1M.svg) and the reproduction steps from content/docs/en/db/benchmarks.mdx in the same repo. Not iso-recall: Zvec recall is 0.9328 (10M) and 0.9164 (1M) versus 0.951 and 0.9528 for Milvus sq8 and 0.9843 and 0.9799 for Milvus HNSW, so the QPS gap partly buys lower recall. Rivals are other VectorDBBench result rows (mixed versions 2.2.12 and 2.5.11, managed Zilliz Cloud at 8 CU) with unequal hardware and a client-server path, while Zvec runs in-process. Zvec version is v0.1.1 (repo is now at v0.7.0). The README only embeds a QPS chart. FAISS is not in this comparison. CPU model not stated, so not tier A.
